Glossary: shell, earthquake catalog, local magnitude, UTC. A pipe (|) sends what one command prints into the next command. Read The Unix Shell (swc_shell), episode 4, 'Pipes and Filters'. Tools: wc, head, cut, grep, sort, tail, ls -l, du.
Glossary: thread, CPU core, memory. Run st.server_rules() in a code cell and read what it prints; docs/server_manners.md explains the rules.

Glossary: repository, upstream, private copy. A remote is a short name for the address of another copy of the repository. Read docs/git_workflow.md, section 'Make your private copy', and Version Control with Git (swc_git), episode 'Remotes in GitHub'.
Read docs/ai_policy.md, section 'The AI log', and the template docs/templates/ai_log_template.md. Glossary: commit, private copy.

Glossary: great_circle_distance, vectorization. The Given formula turns two latitudes and two longitudes into a central angle (the angle between the two points seen from the Earth's center); distance = radius x angle. NumPy's trigonometric functions work in radians: see the angle demo in Part 2, and Harris et al. (2020) on NumPy arrays.

Glossary: kst, utc. KST is always UTC + 9 h, so UTC = KST - 9 h. A datetime.datetime object does calendar arithmetic for you (days, months, leap years) when you subtract a datetime.timedelta. See the tools demo in Part 3.

Look at the Part 4 demos (blank fields, BOM, time zones); McKinney (2010) introduces pandas.

Glossary: great_circle_distance, epicenter, vectorization. Your haversine_km from task 1 takes whole arrays, so one call gives the distance to every event. A boolean array (one True or False per row) selects rows with df[mask] or df.loc[mask], and sort_values orders rows by a column (Part 4 demos).

hints.1: Glossary: kst, utc, time_zone. One moment can be shown on different clocks. Here you turn the same UTC moments into KST in two ways, with a fixed 9-hour offset and with the 'Asia/Seoul' time zone, and look for the rows where the two clocks show different readings. Remember Part 3: an aware time stamp is a moment; a clock reading is what a clock shows at that moment.

hints.1: Concept: an inverse undoes a calculation, the way division undoes multiplication. The natural logarithm np.log undoes e to a power: np.log(np.exp(y)) gives y back. Re-read the small logarithm example above the task, then solve the house rule for M on paper before you write code. Reading: the NumPy documentation of numpy.log, and Harris et al. (2020) for NumPy arrays.

Concept: a pandas Series is one column of values with labels, called its index; here the labels are years. Datetime columns have a .dt accessor that gives parts of each time (look up "pandas dt accessor"). Reading: McKinney (2010).

Concept: one Figure holds one or more Axes, and you draw on an Axes (section 1 of this notebook). Matplotlib understands datetime columns, so origin_utc can go straight in as x. Reading: Hunter (2007) and the Software Carpentry episode on plotting.

Concept: a PyGMT map is built layer by layer on one pygmt.Figure (basemap, coast, plot, text), and a later layer covers an earlier one. Re-read the toy map above and the PyGMT tutorial "Plotting data points". Reading: Wessel et al. (2019).

Concept: great-circle distance (st.glossary.term("great_circle_distance")), which you met in M01. On a sphere of radius 6371 km the haversine formula is accurate enough here. Then reuse your yearly-count function.

Glossary: utc, kst, naive_datetime, aware_datetime, time_window. pandas.to_datetime with utc=True turns text, a Timestamp or a datetime into one UTC moment: it converts times that carry a zone and declares zone-less times UTC. str() of an ObsPy UTCDateTime is ISO text ending in Z. Timestamp.isoformat() keeps the zone. M04 task 2 handled time zeros the same way.

Glossary: station_epoch, epicentral_distance, great_circle_distance. pandas compares dates with <= and >= once on_date is a Timestamp (pandas.Timestamp turns the text into one); Series.isna() finds missing end dates; 'end_date' in df.columns tells whether the column exists. Your M01 distance function works on whole columns at once; DataFrame.assign adds a column to a copy.

hints.1: Glossary: completeness_check, station, network_code, component. pathlib.Path.iterdir() lists a folder, .is_dir() and .is_file() tell folders from files, and str.split('.') cuts a file name into its parts. A dict of sets (station -> set of last letters) collects the components; pandas.DataFrame(0, index=..., columns=...) starts a table of zeros.

Glossary: instrument_response, response_stage, stage_gain, overall_sensitivity, station_epoch, polarity_reversal. An Inventory holds networks, a network holds stations, a station holds channels, and a for loop walks each level; every level has .code, and a channel also has .location_code, .start_date, .end_date and .response.response_stages. Inventory.select(...) with network, station, location, channel and time is allowed too.

Glossary: kst, utc, naive_datetime, envelope, signal_to_noise_ratio. Part 3 showed the catalog rows next to the UTC folder names. Which zone does ObsPy's UTCDateTime assume for a time written without one? datetime.timezone(datetime.timedelta(hours=9)) is a fixed +09:00 zone; Timestamp.tz_localize attaches a zone to a naive time. For the evidence: Trace.slice, Trace.times(reftime=...), obspy.signal.filter.envelope and obspy.geodetics.gps2dist_azimuth.

Glossary: frequency_magnitude_distribution, magnitude_binning, floating_point_number, cumulative_count. Part 3 explains why the bins are centered on multiples of dm and shows what floating-point noise looks like. Mignan & Woessner (2012) draw both kinds of FMD.

Glossary: utc, kst, time_zero. pandas.to_datetime turns text, a Timestamp or a datetime into a time; with utc=True it declares zone-less times UTC and converts the others. pandas.Timedelta(days=...) is a length of time. M01 Part 3 shows aware and naive times.

Glossary: catalog_matching, great_circle_distance. DataFrame.merge with how='cross' pairs every row of one table with every row of another; Series.dt.total_seconds() turns time differences into seconds; epicentral_km works on whole columns at once; a Python set remembers which ids are already taken.

Glossary: magnitude_of_completeness, maximum_curvature, network_epoch. Part 6 states the rule of thumb (Wiemer & Wyss 2000; Woessner & Wiemer 2005). In each panel the blue circles are the counts per bin and the gray squares the cumulative counts.

Glossary: magnitude_binning, floating_point_number, utc. Series.dt.year gives the UTC year of every event. Working in whole tenths (ML times 10, rounded to the nearest whole number) puts every magnitude in its 0.1 bin, noise or not; numpy.isin tests whether values are in a list.

Glossary: fdsn, comcat, quakeml. Part 1 shows Client('USGS').get_events with its arguments and a guarded download with a cached copy. The ObsPy documentation of obspy.clients.fdsn and Krischer et al. (2015) describe the FDSN client.

hints.1: Glossary: maximum_likelihood, b_value, magnitude_binning, standard_error. The estimator is in Part 2 (Aki 1965; Utsu 1965 for the correction); the uncertainty is Shi and Bolt (1982). Mind the base of the logarithm and the float rounding warned about in the Contract.
Glossary: magnitude_of_completeness, maximum_curvature, histogram. Wiemer and Wyss (2000) take the peak of the per-bin FMD; Woessner and Wiemer (2005) add 0.2. The listed values are the bin centers.

Glossary: omori_utsu_law, poisson_process, negative_log_likelihood, numerical_optimization. The log-likelihood and the integral are in Part 5 (Ogata 1983); scipy.optimize.minimize does the search.

Glossary: mainshock, aftershock, magnitude_of_completeness, omori_utsu_law. This task only combines your functions of tasks 2-5 (Parts 2-5). Glossary: declustering, background_seismicity. Gardner and Knopoff (1974); SeismoStats (Mirwald et al. 2026) implements their windows. Part 7 shows the window sizes and the table SeismoStats needs.
